checks.question: Does a Thai food-safety rule restrict or require approval for banana or pandan leaves used as food packaging or in contact with a drink?
checks.finding: No rule found names banana or pandan leaves or bars leaf packaging outright. The only container-specific MOPH rule found is Notification No. 92 (B.E. 2528, 1985). Per a FAOLEX summary, its clauses 4 to 6 set general quality rules (no harmful release of heavy metals or other contaminants into food) and clause 7 bars reuse of containers previously used for fertilizer, poison or harmful substances. Its title also includes 'prohibition of use of things as food containers', and the list of prohibited things could not be read: the FAOLEX PDF is an unreadable scan, and the DSS copy returned HTTP 523. A TCI journal article (2020) says Notification 92 does not define 'container'. Plastic container rules (Notification No. 435, B.E. 2565, replacing No. 295) cover plastic only. A DSS voluntary specification for areca-sheath food containers (DSS7-2566) shows natural-leaf containers are handled through voluntary standards; its full text was not readable here, and a search summary says it is not a mandatory legal standard. A 2026 draft food-contact revision covers ceramics, metals, glass, paper and board, and the article describing it does not mention natural materials. Verdict is unresolved because the Notification 92 prohibition list could not be read.

checks.question: Can the pack carry a 'plastic-free' or 'eco' claim in Thailand, and which rule applies?
checks.finding: No Thai rule found bans or specifically regulates 'plastic-free' or 'eco' wording on food packaging, and Thailand has no statute aimed specifically at greenwashing. The general rules that would apply are: (1) Food Act B.E. 2522 s.40, which prohibits advertising a food's benefits, quality or effects as false or deceptively misleading (penalty up to 3 years and/or 30,000 baht under s.70, per a secondary article); whether a packaging environmental claim counts as a food benefit or quality is not settled. (2) Food Act s.41, which requires prior review of certain food advertising for commerce; whether it reaches packaging claims is not settled, the 2008 rule found is in a folder marked CANCEL, and a 2021 (B.E. 2564) FDA food advertising rule was located but not read. (3) Consumer Protection Act B.E. 2522 s.22, which bars false or exaggerated advertising (read only through secondary summaries). A search summary says the Food Act's definition of 'label' covers marks and text on the container or packaging. A plastic-free claim is only lawful if accurate: if the pack carries any plastic film (the kill test's inner-film case), the claim would be false. The TEI Green Label is voluntary. EU rules restricting 'eco-friendly' claims (ECGT, applying from 27 Sept 2026) bind only EU-market sales. Verdict is unresolved because the governing rule for packaging claims (s.40 vs s.41 vs Consumer Protection Act s.22) and the current FDA advertising rule text are not settled.

checks.question: Under Thai FDA rules, is a drink with added isoflavone extract classified as a food or as a food supplement? What registration route applies to each?
checks.finding: Notification No. 293 (B.E. 2548), clause 2, defines a food supplement as a product taken in addition to the normal diet, containing nutrients or other substances, in tablet, capsule, powder, liquid or other forms that are NOT conventional food forms, for consumers expecting health-promotion benefits. The compiled text shows no amendment footnote on clause 2; clauses 4, 9, 10 and 12 were replaced by Notifications 405 (B.E. 2562) and 411 (B.E. 2562). On the public definition, a 250 ml UHT soy drink in conventional drink form falls outside the food-supplement definition and sits on the food route. Caveats: the current consolidated text of 405, 411 and 448 (B.E. 2566, food supplement no. 5) was not retrieved; the Thai FDA PDF of No. 448 could not be located (404 on tried URLs), and secondary sources disagree on its effective date (17 Jun 2024 vs 2 Jul 2024). Registration route: under 293 clause 12, a supplement label must show the food serial number (เลขสารบบอาหาร). The route for a conventional food with added isoflavone extract (food serial number only, or any extra safety or novel-food review under Notification 447 clause 2(1)(1)) was not settled from public text. A secondary vendor page says supplements fall under a 'specifically controlled food' route; this was not verified against a primary text.

checks.question: Can a food or a supplement in Thailand carry a menopause, hot-flush or sleep benefit claim, and which notification sets the wording? Verdict kill if the rules bar a menopause-linked benefit on a food.
checks.finding: Notification No. 447 (B.E. 2566), health claims on food labels, governs wording. Annexes 1 to 3 list nutrient function claims, a short list of other function claims (beta-glucans, phytosterols/phytostanols, choline, DHA/EPA, sodium, saturated fat) and disease-risk claims. None concerns soy, isoflavones, menopause, hot flushes or sleep. The FDA's later annex adds four items (cocoa flavanols, native chicory inulin, fructo-oligosaccharides, and monounsaturated fat replacing saturated fat), none on soy or menopause. Clause 5: a claim not in Annexes 1 to 3 may be used only after assessment by a Thai FDA-recognised nutrition and health claim assessment centre and approval by the FDA. So the rules do not bar a menopause-linked claim outright, and a route exists. However, clause 6(2) prohibits claims that mislead consumers about treatment, relief, cure or prevention of disease, and clause 6(3)(7) requires the statement 'Not intended to treat, relieve, cure or prevent any disease' on other function claims. Whether hot-flush or sleep symptoms count as a 'disease' for the clause 6(2) relief bar is not settled by the text. Clause 2(3) requires well-designed human intervention studies in the target group, and clause 6(3)(5) requires any maximum safe intake statement. Food-supplement claim wording (293 as amended, 448) was not retrieved. The kill test is not met on the text (no explicit bar and an assessment route exists), but the clause 6(2) relief bar is an open risk for a menopause or hot-flush claim. Verdict unresolved.

checks.question: What upper-intake or safety guidance exists for isoflavones (Thai FDA, Singapore HPB or EFSA), and does it cap a labelled dose in a daily drink?
checks.finding: No binding Thai, EFSA or Singapore cap on a labelled isoflavone dose in a daily food was found. EFSA (press release, 21 Oct 2015) found no indication of harm at isoflavone levels typically found in food supplements over 3 months to just under 1 year; it stated no tolerable upper intake level and no safe maximum daily intake, and noted no data for women in transition to menopause or with a personal or family history of cancer. Those gaps cover part of the target group (women aged 40 to 59). No Thai FDA isoflavone intake limit was found. Mahidol pharmacy knowledge page (undated, non-binding) suggests 50 to 100 mg isoflavones per day as an intake guide. A 2005 Japanese food-safety panel, reported secondarily, set about 70 to 75 mg per day from food and supplements and judged about 30 mg per day from supplements acceptable (old, non-binding). Singapore HPB guidance was not found. Product variation (25.5 to 63.5 mg per 250 ml across four Thai soy-milk brands) means a labelled dose needs verification. Verdict unresolved: no cap was found, but safety for the target group is not settled.

checks.question: What do the Thai alcohol-advertising rules (Alcohol Control Act B.E. 2551 and its advertising provisions) say about a non-alcoholic product that positions itself as an alcohol alternative or uses alcohol-like cues? Kill only if the rule bars that positioning outright; otherwise unresolved with section cited.
checks.finding: Unresolved, with sections cited. No provision found bars an alcohol-alternative positioning outright. Amended Act (No. 2, B.E. 2568): section 32/3 is the relevant clause. It prohibits indirect advertising, including using alcohol brand names, logos or symbols on non-alcoholic products where the use could reasonably be seen as promoting alcoholic beverages. Section 32/1 generally prohibits advertising of alcoholic beverages, with exceptions for factual, educational or public communication under Ministerial conditions. Section 32/2 bars celebrity and influencer endorsement that displays alcohol brand names or trademarks. The original 2008 section 32 (first paragraph, per secondary summaries) barred direct or indirect promotion using alcohol names or symbols that highlight attributes or induce drinking. Under the amended text, a non-alcoholic product with its own brand, no alcohol marks, and only alcohol-like cues (flavour, can design, beer-style naming) is not barred on its face. The 32/3 test is fact-dependent, not an outright bar. Gaps: the law-firm summary says the Act does not define 'alcoholic beverage' or give an alcohol-percentage threshold, so whether a near-zero product falls within the Act is unverified. Ministerial conditions under 32/1 and 32/2 were still being drafted; a public consultation on a draft under 32/1 was reported for 9 September 2026. The draft reportedly restricts bottle and packaging images and sets media limits. No information was found on how the draft treats non-alcoholic products. The Royal Gazette PDFs are binary and could not be read, so section wording comes from secondary summaries. Effective date: 8 November 2025 (60 days after 9 September 2025 publication), per the law-firm page and a Thai press excerpt; one Thai excerpt says 90 days.
